title: Abbasid Caliphate/Buyid Dynasty
capsule: This composite entry marks the specific quarter-century, from Mu'izz al-Dawla's decisive 947 victory over the rival Hamdanids of Mosul to Caliph al-Muti's incapacitating stroke in 970, when the Buyid amir of Iraq and the Abbasid caliph functioned as a single, tightly bound governing apparatus in Baghdad. Mu'izz al-Dawla (amir 945-967), who had installed al-Muti as a compliant replacement for the blinded al-Mustakfi in 946, kept the caliph under close watch, confiscated the former caliphal crown domains to pay his troops, and reduced al-Muti to a ceremonial figure retaining only religious legitimacy. His son Izz al-Dawla Bakhtiyar (amir 967-978) inherited this arrangement in 967, continuing the caliph's formal investiture of Buyid authority until al-Muti's declining health forced his abdication in 974, shortly after this window closes.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases (Times Atlas of World History; Kinder & Hilgemann; Shepherd 1926) at ~0.07° resolution. The mapped polity is the caliphs' direct Iraqi domain, far smaller than their nominal suzerainty. Confidence: high for the domain; the wider claim is unmappable by design.
